ABOn Circumcircle

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: a triangle sits on a circle, and the lines that split its corners in half meet the circle again.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B and C, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the names, the right angle or the hint.
Look for the math

Drag a corner and the whole picture changes, yet three things stay true: each line that halves a corner cuts an arc exactly in half, all three lines pass through one point, and one of them meets the line joining the other two points at a right angle.

Halving an arc

The line that splits the corner at A in half meets the circumcircle again at D. Because the two small angles at A are equal, the two arcs they cut off are equal: D is the midpoint of the arc BC. The same goes for E and F. Equal arcs give equal chords, so BD = CD, CE = AE and AF = BF. This is the inscribed angle idea: angles that stand on equal arcs are equal.

Where the three lines meet

Intersection of the three angle bisectors is the incenter I. It lies on all three lines AD, BE and CF, and it is the same distance from each side of the triangle. Here I is found as the side-length-weighted average of the corners, and the logic test checks that it really lies on all three bisectors.

Why AD is perpendicular to EF

Let M be where AD crosses EF. In the triangle FIM, the angle at F is ∠IFM = ∠CFE = ∠CBE = B/2 — equal inscribed angles again. The exterior angle at I is ∠FIM = ∠ACI + ∠CAI = C/2 + A/2. So two angles of triangle FIM add to A/2 + B/2 + C/2 = 90°, and the last angle, at M, must be a right angle. The old page's claim is true: AD ⟂ EF, and its two siblings BE ⟂ FD and CF ⟂ DE hold too.

What the checks found

The logic test tries seven exact triangles and hundreds of generated ones, including obtuse and almost flat ones. On every one it finds the equal arcs, the common incenter, the right angle at M and the angle identities above, all to within a millionth. It also rebuilds the whole construction a second way, straight from the old applet's bytecode, and checks that both ways give the same D, E, F, I and M.

Try dragging B down until the triangle is nearly flat: AD and EF still meet at a right angle.
